title: 25 Habits That Keep People Broke (Without Them Noticing)
description:
Most people who stay broke aren't lazy. They work hard and pay their bills, and the money still disappears every month. In this video I go through 25 quiet habits that keep people broke, from three angles: the numbers you can measure, the psychology that keeps you spending without noticing, and the playbook of simple systems that turn it around.

Get The Ryan Rover Money Playbook: [LINK HERE]

1:36 How we got the numbers
2:06 Angle 1: The Numbers
2:12 1. Not knowing where the money goes

4:32 4. Financing everything
5:19 5. Ignoring small subscriptions
6:03 6. Eating out by default
6:46 7. Keeping cash in a zero interest account
7:33 8. Paying late
8:16 9. Buying new when used works
8:59 Why small leaks sink big ships

11:09 10. Treating windfalls as fun money
11:55 11. Rewarding yourself constantly
12:40 12. Keeping up with friends

14:05 14. Avoiding money completely
15:03 15. Believing it's too late
15:41 16. Believing more income will fix it
16:23 17. Believing money is for other people
17:02 Why your brain fights saving
18:27 Angle 3: The Playbook
18:43 18. No emergency fund
19:23 19. Saving what's left over
20:01 20. Skipping the employer match
20:37 21. Never investing
21:21 22. No written goals
21:58 23. Never asking for more
22:40 24. Not protecting what you have

23:59 Two paychecks, two stories
25:55 The habits that replace them
27:34 Your 4 week reset
28:12 Where to start at your age
29:11 Questions people ask
31:20 Recap: all 25
32:12 What to do next

Sources:
- Federal Reserve, Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2024 (SHED): 63% would cover a $400 emergency expense with cash or its equivalent
- Federal Reserve, G.19 Consumer Credit: interest rate on credit card accounts assessed interest (above 20%)
- Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, research on overdraft and NSF fee revenue
- Edmunds, average new-vehicle monthly payment (above $700 in recent years)
- US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Expenditure Survey (food away from home)
- IRS filing season statistics (average federal refund around $3,000)
- Richard Thaler, mental accounting; Daniel Kahneman, behavioral economics
- Thomas J. Stanley and William D. Danko, The Millionaire Next Door (first-generation wealth)
- Growth examples: monthly compounding at 7% average yearly return (illustration, not a promise)
